words.definition: a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time
words.example: A population of deer may occupy one forest.

words.definition: the total number of individuals in a population
words.example: Population size can change through births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

words.definition: the number of individuals per unit area or volume
words.example: Population density is useful when comparing habitats of different sizes.

words.definition: sampling in which locations or individuals are selected without intentional bias
words.example: Random sampling helps produce representative ecological data.

words.definition: a frame defining a known area used to sample organisms, especially sessile species
words.example: Quadrats can estimate plant abundance in grassland.

words.definition: change in population size over time
words.example: Population growth is positive when additions exceed losses.

words.definition: the maximum population size that an environment can sustain over time under given conditions
words.example: Resource limitation can cause a population to stabilize near carrying capacity.

words.definition: all populations of different species living and interacting in an area
words.example: A pond community includes plants, animals and microorganisms.

words.definition: an interaction in which an animal consumes plant or algal tissue
words.example: Herbivory can reduce plant biomass.

words.definition: an interaction in which one organism captures and consumes another
words.example: Predation can influence both predator and prey population sizes.

words.definition: competition for resources between individuals of different species
words.example: Interspecific competition may reduce the realized niche of a species.

words.definition: an interaction between species in which both partners benefit
words.example: Pollination can be a mutualism between flowering plants and insects.

words.definition: an interaction in which a parasite benefits while harming its host
words.example: A tapeworm obtains nutrients through parasitism.

words.definition: the biological relationship between a disease-causing organism and the host it infects
words.example: A pathogen-host interaction may influence survival and reproduction of both populations.

words.definition: a non-native species that spreads and causes ecological or other harm
words.example: An invasive species may reduce native biodiversity.

words.definition: a species naturally restricted to a particular geographic area
words.example: Island ecosystems often contain many endemic species.

words.definition: a non-random relationship in the occurrence or abundance of species
words.example: A positive ecological association may suggest that two species use similar conditions.

words.definition: a statistical test used to compare observed frequencies with expected frequencies
words.example: A chi-squared test can assess whether two categorical ecological variables are associated.

words.definition: a method for estimating mobile population size by capturing, marking, releasing and later recapturing individuals
words.example: Capture-mark-release-recapture can estimate the number of fish in a pond.

words.definition: an estimator of population size based on proportions of marked and unmarked individuals in recapture samples
words.example: The Lincoln index assumes marked individuals mix randomly back into the population.

words.definition: the difference between a sample estimate and the true population value caused by chance selection
words.example: Increasing sample size can reduce sampling error.

words.definition: a factor whose effect on a population changes with population density
words.example: Competition often becomes stronger as population density rises.

words.definition: a factor that affects populations largely regardless of their density
words.example: A severe storm can act as a density-independent factor.

words.definition: population growth at a constant proportional rate, producing a J-shaped curve under ideal conditions
words.example: A small microbial population may show exponential growth when resources are abundant.

words.definition: population growth that slows as carrying capacity is approached, producing an S-shaped curve
words.example: Sigmoid growth can occur when density-dependent limits increase.

words.definition: competition for resources among individuals of the same species
words.example: Intraspecific competition often increases as a population becomes crowded.

words.definition: interaction in which individuals work together in ways that can improve survival or reproduction
words.example: Cooperation can improve hunting success in some social predators.

words.definition: regulation of lower trophic levels by consumers at higher trophic levels
words.example: Predators can exert top-down control on herbivore populations.

words.definition: regulation of higher trophic levels by availability of resources at lower trophic levels
words.example: Nutrient availability can cause bottom-up control of food webs.

units.unit: C4.2 Transfers of energy and matter

words.definition: a community of organisms and the abiotic environment with which they interact
words.example: An ecosystem includes both living organisms and physical conditions.

words.definition: a system that exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings
words.example: Most ecosystems are open systems.

words.definition: a system that exchanges energy but little or no matter with its surroundings
words.example: A sealed ecological model can approximate a closed system for matter.

words.definition: the one-way transfer of energy through organisms and trophic levels
words.example: Energy flow begins with an external energy source and decreases between trophic levels.

words.definition: a linear sequence showing transfer of energy and matter by feeding
words.example: A food chain may run from grass to rabbit to fox.

words.definition: a network of interconnected food chains in a community
words.example: A food web shows that most species have multiple feeding relationships.

words.definition: a feeding position in a food chain or food web
words.example: Producers occupy the first trophic level.

words.definition: an autotroph that converts external energy into chemical energy stored in organic matter
words.example: Green plants are producers in terrestrial ecosystems.

words.definition: a consumer that feeds directly on producers
words.example: A grazing rabbit is a primary consumer.

words.definition: a consumer that feeds on primary consumers
words.example: A snake eating a herbivorous mouse can act as a secondary consumer.

words.definition: a consumer that feeds on secondary consumers
words.example: A top predator may act as a tertiary consumer.

words.definition: a diagram showing energy available or transferred at successive trophic levels
words.japanese: エネルギーピラミッド
words.example: An energy pyramid narrows because energy is lost between trophic levels.

words.definition: energy that leaves a trophic transfer pathway, often through respiration, heat, waste or uneaten material
words.example: Respiration contributes substantially to energy loss between trophic levels.

words.definition: the mass of living biological material in a given area, volume or trophic level
words.example: Plant biomass forms the main energy store at the base of many terrestrial food webs.

words.definition: the production of organic matter by autotrophs
words.example: Photosynthesis drives primary production in most ecosystems.

words.definition: the production of new consumer biomass from assimilated food
words.example: Growth of herbivores contributes to secondary production.

words.definition: repeated movement and reuse of mineral nutrients between organisms and the abiotic environment
words.example: Decomposition is important for nutrient cycling.

words.definition: the movement of carbon among organisms, atmosphere, water, soils and rocks
words.example: Photosynthesis and respiration are major processes in the carbon cycle.

words.definition: a reservoir or process that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a period
words.example: A growing forest can act as a carbon sink.

words.definition: a reservoir or process that releases more carbon than it absorbs over a period
words.example: Burning fossil fuels is a major carbon source to the atmosphere.

words.definition: rapid oxidation of a fuel that releases energy and usually produces carbon dioxide when carbon compounds burn completely
words.example: Combustion of fossil fuels transfers stored carbon to the atmosphere.

words.definition: the long-term record showing the rise and seasonal variation of atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa
words.example: The Keeling Curve provides evidence of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide.

words.definition: an autotroph that obtains energy by oxidizing inorganic substances rather than from light
words.japanese: 化学合成独立栄養生物
words.example: Some bacteria are chemoautotrophs at hydrothermal vents.

words.definition: an organism that consumes dead organic material and associated microorganisms
words.example: Woodlice act as detritus feeders in leaf litter.

words.definition: incorporation of absorbed nutrients into an organism's own tissues and molecules
words.example: Only part of ingested food energy is assimilated into consumer tissues.

words.definition: light used as the initial energy input for a biological or ecological process
words.example: Sunlight is the main light energy source for most ecosystems.

words.definition: energy stored in chemical bonds and molecular arrangements
words.example: Chemical energy in organic molecules is transferred through food webs.

words.definition: the proportion of input energy converted into a desired output or transferred to the next trophic level
words.example: Trophic transfer has limited energy efficiency because organisms use energy in respiration.
